newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope opens Vatican celebrations in run-up to 2000.
newsitem.headline: Pope opens Vatican celebrations in run-up to 2000.

text.p: Pope John Paul called for greater unity between the Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches on Saturday when he opened celebrations leading up to the year 2000, the start of the third Christian millennium.

The Pope, who has declared 2000 a holy year, launched three years of preparations for the Vatican's celebration at the end of the century in a vespers ceremony that also marked the start of Advent, the period leading up to Christmas.

"The millenia belong to Christ, especially the two which mark his coming to the world and whose anniversary we shall celebrate," the Pope, who looked tired but in relatively good shape after appendix surgery last month, told pilgrims at St Peter's Basilica.
The preparations "will take us to the threshold of the Holy Door, which I shall open, God willing, on Christmas eve, 1999", added the Pope, referring to the doors of St Peter's.

He said Christians should spend the last three years of the century preparing themselves spiritually for the new millenium and called on humanity to show a stronger social conscience and more brotherly love.

The ceremony was carried out according to an ancient rite common both to Catholic and Eastern liturgy in which the lights of the church are suddenly turned on to symbolise "Christ, the light of the world".

The Pope, 76, who has made Christian unity a primary goal of the run-up to the year 2000, sent a letter on Saturday to Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew I, the leader of the world's Orthodox Christians.
The Pope said in the letter that he hoped Christians could arrive at the year 2000 "if not united, at least closer to resolving the divisions of the second millenium".

"Today, at the threshold of the third millenium of our history, we want the Christian communities...to open themselves up to the appeal of the spirit, which is guiding Christians to a full and visible unity," he said.
Bartholomew I, who made a historic visit to the Vatican in June 1995, was only the third Orthodox leader to meet a Pope since the churches split in the Great Schism of 1054.
The two leaders issued a joint statement after that meeting pledging that the world's 950 million Catholics and 150 million Orthodox Christians would seek greater unity as the year 2000 approaches.
They also said improved ties would help the cause of peace and issued an appeal to save the environment and for Eastern European countries to be allowed to join the European Union.

The Pope said in his letter that the effort to improve relations "has been a source of great joy and has borne fruit" even if the dialogue between the two churches was still "slow and laborious" and "the road to travel was still very long".

On Thursday, Russian Orthodox officials said it was still too early for the Polish Pope to visit Russia, although the Catholic church was seen as coming round to Moscow's view that it should not encroach on Orthodox territory.
Last July, the Vatican announced a possible papal meeting with Patriarch Alexiy, head of the Russian church, but has made it clear that the time was not ripe.

Tensions between the two denominations stem in part from disputes over property confiscated from the Catholic Church and passed to the Russian Orthodox Church under communist rule in Russia and the former Soviet republics.
